analysis.title: US rates and a triple whammy of obstacles to overcome
key_insights: ING sees the US 10yr Treasury yield rising to about 5.25% in the first part of 2027, possibly 5.50%, versus 4.9% currently, then falling to 4.50-4.75% later in 2027 as inflation eases.

Three drivers push yields up through Q1 2027: AI-related productivity growth and issuance (the 'good'), elevated fiscal deficits (the 'bad') and sticky inflation (the 'ugly'). The same dynamics apply in France, Japan and the UK.

The real yield is the main driver of nominal yields. Inflation expectations (10yr Treasury yield minus 10yr TIPS real yield) rarely swing much, so real yield moves set the direction of nominal yields.

AI contributes about a fifth of the move in long rates. ING warns that AI-related debt issuance pressure could begin to outweigh AI productivity gains in 2027, because the crowding-out effect grows as outstanding debt rises.

Higher printed inflation shows up partly in real yields as a larger term premium. The fiscal deficit has a similar effect through Treasury supply and through investors' perception of, and the price they will pay for, Treasuries.

US swap spreads have tightened, partly because Treasury Secretary Bessent increased long-end buybacks with the implied threat of more. Fast-money accounts have also gone long Treasuries and paid in swaps against an implied cap on swap spreads.

ING would fade the swap spread tightening absent an aggressive Treasury move to cancel long-end auctions or add buybacks. It expects the 10yr swap spread to re-widen to 50bp-plus (now below 40bp) and the 30yr to 75bp at least through 2027, or at least through Q1.
ING says the February 2026 bond sell-off was sparked by the Iran war through elevated printed inflation. The current market has not priced a material rate-cut cycle.

The biggest 2027 risk is inflation failing to ease enough to comfort central banks or bond markets. ING sees this risk reflected in current central bank rate pricing, while longer-tenor inflation expectations are benign.
ING does not want to play the bond-bullish trade too early in 2027, because upward inflation pressure is still in focus heading into the year.

ING does not forecast a 10yr yield of 6%, but identifies three routes to it: GDP growth of 3-4% (real yield from below 3% to about 4%), a deficit widening from the 6-6.5% range to 7-8%, or inflation staying near 3% or worsening (for example from a severe El Niño).

The baseline caps the 10yr at 5.5% because GDP growth and inflation are expected to settle in a 2%-plus range in 2027 with a stable debt narrative. Falling inflation lets the Fed step back and the market re-discount cuts, targeting 4.75% first and then 4.5-4.75%.

A material cut in long-end Treasury issuance would be the key discretionary change, tempering the deficit effect. ING sees it reserved for market stress or systemic threat, where de facto yield curve control might be an option, and does not expect it.

macro_indicators.interpretation: Current level that ING expects to rise toward 5.25% in early 2027.
ING baseline for the peak, with 5.25% most likely and 5.50% the cap.
Expected decline as inflation eases and the market re-discounts Fed rate cuts. 4.75% is the first target.
A rise toward 4% on 3-4% GDP growth would take the nominal 10yr to about 6%.

macro_indicators.indicator: US 10yr swap spread (Treasury yield minus SOFR swap rate)
macro_indicators.interpretation: ING expects it to re-widen to the 50bp-plus area through 2027.
ING expects the 30yr spread to move back up to at least this level.
Stable but elevated. A rise to 7-8% is one route to a 6% 10yr yield.
Sticky inflation near 3% that does not fall is one route to a 6% 10yr yield.

trade_ideas.description: Fade the tightening in US swap spreads: position for re-widening of the 10yr swap spread to 50bp-plus and the 30yr to 75bp
trade_ideas.rationale: Swap spreads should come under re-widening pressure through 2027, or at least through Q1, absent an aggressive Treasury decision to cancel long-end auctions or add to buybacks.
trade_ideas.risk: An aggressive Treasury decision to cancel some long-end auctions and/or add to buybacks.

trade_ideas.description: Avoid positioning bond-bullish too early in 2027
trade_ideas.rationale: Upward pressure on inflation remains in focus into 2027, and a bearish inflation case would deny bond markets relief.
trade_ideas.risk: Inflation falls faster than expected and the market re-discounts Fed rate cuts earlier.

risk_factors: Inflation does not ease enough to comfort central banks or bond markets in 2027.
Elevated fiscal deficits, with the risk that markets quickly reprice debt dynamics before a tipping point, as with Greece a decade and a half ago.
AI-related debt issuance crowding out and eclipsing AI productivity gains.
GDP growth accelerating to 3-4% and lifting real yields.
A severe El Niño pushing inflation higher.
Ad hoc US Treasury changes, such as a material cut in long-dated issuance sizes.
vol_and_positioning: Fast-money players are long Treasuries and paying fixed in swaps, taking advantage of an implied cap on swap spreads, which has tightened US swap spreads further.
geopolitical: The Iran war was the spark for the February 2026 bond sell-off through higher printed inflation.

tension_points.bull_case: Inflation eases later in 2027 and the Fed steps away, so the market re-discounts rate cuts and the 10yr falls to 4.5-4.75%.
tension_points.bear_case: Inflation stays sticky near 3% or worsens, the deficit widens or growth accelerates, which could take the 10yr to 6%.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Inflation failing to ease enough to comfort central banks, GDP growth reaching 3-4%, or the deficit moving to 7-8%.

tension_points.bull_case: Spreads stay tight as Treasury long-end buybacks and fast-money longs in Treasuries with payers in swaps cap them.
tension_points.bear_case: Spreads re-widen to 50bp-plus on the 10yr and 75bp on the 30yr through 2027 on deficit and supply pressure.
tension_points.what_invalidates: An aggressive Treasury decision to cancel some long-end auctions and/or add to buybacks.
